CourseName: CEN3722 - Introduction to Human Computer Interfaces

Outcomes.Text: Explain the foundational concepts of Human-Computer Interaction and their relevance to modern software design.
Identify the key tools used in collaborative HCI design and development, including GitHub, Figma, and AI assistants.
Apply version control principles by setting up and using a GitHub repository for a team project.
Demonstrate proficiency in creating and sharing a collaborative design workspace in Figma.
Analyze how AI tools support the software development lifecycle and apply them responsibly in a course project context.
Create a fully configured team project environment ready for collaborative design and development work.

Topics.Title: Introduction to Human-Computer Interaction
Topics.Summary: Establishes the foundational concepts of HCI and explains why designing for the human experience is central to software development. Students gain shared vocabulary and mental models before moving into tooling and project setup.

Elements.Title: What Is HCI?
Elements.BodyText: Human-Computer Interaction is the study of how people interact with computers and how to design those interactions to be effective, efficient, and satisfying.
Elements.Notes: HCI sits at the intersection of computer science, behavioral science, and design. Emphasize that every interface decision—from button placement to error messages—affects real users.

Items.Text: HCI examines the relationship between users, tasks, and technology systems.
Good HCI reduces cognitive load and increases user satisfaction.
HCI principles apply to web apps, mobile apps, desktop software, and embedded systems.

Elements.Title: Core HCI Principles
Elements.BodyText: Several foundational principles guide HCI practice, including usability, accessibility, feedback, and consistency.
Elements.Notes: These principles come from decades of research and underpin major design frameworks like Nielsen's heuristics. Use everyday app examples to make these concrete.

Items.Text: Usability measures how easily users can achieve their goals with a system.
Accessibility ensures systems are usable by people with a wide range of abilities.
Feedback gives users confirmation that their actions have had the intended effect.
Consistency across interface elements reduces the learning curve for new users.

Elements.Title: The User-Centered Design Process
Elements.BodyText: User-Centered Design (UCD) is an iterative design framework that places the user's needs, goals, and limitations at the forefront of each design decision.
Elements.Notes: UCD typically cycles through research, ideation, prototyping, and testing. Stress that this course project will follow a simplified version of this cycle across the weeks.

Items.Text: UCD begins with understanding users through research such as interviews and observations.
Design solutions are prototyped and tested with real or representative users.
Iteration based on user feedback is a core feature of UCD, not an optional step.
The process reduces costly redesigns by catching usability problems early.

Elements.Title: HCI and the Software Development Lifecycle
Elements.BodyText: HCI considerations appear at every stage of software development, from planning and design through testing and maintenance.
Elements.Notes: Connecting HCI to the SDLC helps students see that UX work is not separate from engineering—it is integrated throughout. Reference how AI tools are now supporting design and testing phases as well.

Items.Text: Requirements gathering benefits from HCI methods like personas and user stories.
Prototyping and usability testing occur during the design and development phases.
Post-launch analytics and user feedback inform ongoing HCI improvements.

Elements.Title: Why HCI Matters for This Course
Elements.BodyText: This course applies HCI principles directly through a team project that spans design, prototyping, and development using industry tools.
Elements.Notes: Frame this as motivation: students are not just learning concepts in isolation—they are building a real artifact that must be usable and well-designed. The toolchain they set up in week one will carry them through the entire course.

Items.Text: The course project provides hands-on experience applying HCI principles to a real interface.
Students will use the same tools—Figma and GitHub—that industry professionals use.
Peer collaboration mirrors real-world cross-functional design and development teams.

Topics.Title: Version Control with GitHub
Topics.Summary: Introduces GitHub as the central collaboration and code management platform for the course project. Students set up repositories, learn branching strategies, and understand how GitHub supports team workflows.

Elements.Title: What Is Version Control?
Elements.BodyText: Version control is a system that records changes to files over time, allowing teams to track history, collaborate without conflict, and revert to earlier states when needed.
Elements.Notes: Use an analogy like 'tracked changes in a document' but for entire codebases. Emphasize that version control is non-negotiable on professional teams.

Items.Text: Version control preserves a complete history of every change made to a project.
Multiple contributors can work simultaneously without overwriting each other's work.
Any version of the project can be restored at any point in its history.

Elements.Title: GitHub as a Collaboration Platform
Elements.BodyText: GitHub is the world's most widely adopted developer platform, providing cloud-hosted Git repositories alongside tools for project planning, code review, and team communication.
Elements.Notes: GitHub is used by millions of developers and major organizations including Mercedes-Benz, Shopify, and Spotify. Highlight that GitHub also integrates AI assistance through GitHub Copilot, which students may use in this course.

Items.Text: GitHub hosts repositories in the cloud, making code accessible from any device.
Built-in tools like Issues, Projects, and Discussions support full project management.
GitHub Actions enables automated workflows such as testing and deployment pipelines.
GitHub Copilot provides AI-powered code suggestions directly inside the development environment.

Elements.Title: Creating and Configuring a Repository
Elements.BodyText: Each team will create a shared GitHub repository that serves as the single source of truth for all project code and documentation.
Elements.Notes: Walk students through creating a repo, adding a README, selecting a .gitignore template, and choosing a license. Stress that a clear README sets expectations for all contributors from day one.

Items.Text: A repository stores all project files, commit history, and collaboration metadata.
The README file should describe the project purpose, setup instructions, and contributor guidelines.
A .gitignore file prevents unnecessary or sensitive files from being tracked.
Access permissions control who can read, write, or administer the repository.

Elements.Title: Branching and Pull Requests
Elements.BodyText: Branching allows team members to develop features or fixes in isolation before merging changes into the main codebase through a pull request review process.
Elements.Notes: Introduce a simple branching convention for the course, such as main for stable code and feature branches named by feature or student. Pull requests create a record of what changed and why.

Items.Text: The main branch should always contain stable, working code.
Feature branches isolate new work from the main branch until it is reviewed and approved.
A pull request invites teammates to review, comment on, and approve proposed changes.
Merging integrates approved changes and maintains a clean project history.

Elements.Title: GitHub for Project Management
Elements.BodyText: Beyond code, GitHub provides Issues and Projects boards that help teams track tasks, assign responsibilities, and monitor progress throughout the course.
Elements.Notes: Encourage teams to create issues for each project task from the start. This mirrors Agile and Scrum practices used in industry and keeps accountability transparent.

Items.Text: GitHub Issues function as task tickets that can be assigned, labeled, and linked to code changes.
Project boards visualize work in columns such as To Do, In Progress, and Done.
Milestones group related issues to track progress toward major project deliverables.

Topics.Title: Design Collaboration with Figma
Topics.Summary: Introduces Figma as the primary design and prototyping tool for the course project. Students set up an education team workspace and learn how Figma supports ideation, UI design, and design-to-code handoff.

Elements.Title: What Is Figma?
Elements.BodyText: Figma is a browser-based, multiplayer design tool used by professional designers and engineers to create graphics, wireframes, interactive prototypes, and design systems.
Elements.Notes: Figma is free for students and educators through the Figma Education plan. Students should sign up with their school email and verify their student status to unlock all professional features at no cost.

Items.Text: Figma runs entirely in the browser, requiring no software installation.
Multiple collaborators can edit the same file simultaneously in real time.
Figma is used by professionals across design, engineering, and product roles.
The Education plan provides free access to all paid professional features for verified students and teachers.

Elements.Title: Setting Up the Education Team Workspace
Elements.BodyText: Students must create a Figma account with their school email, verify their student status, and join or create a team workspace to unlock free professional collaboration features.
Elements.Notes: Steps: (1) Create account at figma.com using school email. (2) Verify student or educator status through Figma's verification page. (3) Create or join an Education team. Teams should be created once per project group.

Items.Text: Using a school email address is required to qualify for the free Education plan.
Verification unlocks unlimited projects, version history, and advanced prototyping tools.
An Education team workspace allows all members to collaborate on shared project files.

Elements.Title: FigJam for Ideation and Brainstorming
Elements.BodyText: FigJam is an online whiteboard tool within the Figma ecosystem designed for brainstorming, diagramming, and collaborative planning activities.
Elements.Notes: FigJam is well-suited for early-stage HCI activities like affinity mapping, user journey mapping, and design critiques. It supports sticky notes, stamps, voting, audio chat, and cursor chat.

Items.Text: FigJam enables teams to brainstorm ideas together using sticky notes, shapes, and images.
Real-time features like cursor chat and voting facilitate active group participation.
FigJam files can be linked directly to Figma design files to keep ideation and execution connected.

Elements.Title: Designing UI with Figma
Elements.BodyText: Figma's design canvas allows teams to create wireframes, high-fidelity mockups, and interactive prototypes that simulate the final user experience.
Elements.Notes: Students can use community templates and component libraries to accelerate their design work. Prototypes can be shared with a link, making it easy to conduct lightweight usability tests even before any code is written.

Items.Text: Frames and components in Figma mirror the structure of real web and mobile interfaces.
Interactive prototypes connect screens with clickable transitions to simulate user flows.
Community templates and shared component libraries speed up the design process.
Feedback and comments can be added directly on the canvas without leaving Figma.

Elements.Title: Dev Mode: Bridging Design and Code
Elements.BodyText: Figma's Dev Mode workspace allows developers to inspect designs and extract precise measurements, styles, and auto-generated code snippets, reducing miscommunication between design and development.
Elements.Notes: Dev Mode is especially valuable for students learning how design concepts map to CSS and component properties. It can generate CSS, iOS, and Android code snippets from any design element.

Items.Text: Dev Mode provides exact spacing, typography, and color values from any design element.
Auto-generated CSS and framework-specific code snippets give developers a head start.
Developers can compare design versions to understand what changed between iterations.

Topics.Title: AI Tools in HCI and Development
Topics.Summary: Surveys how AI tools are being used across the design and development workflow and establishes responsible guidelines for using AI assistance during the course project.

Elements.Title: How AI Supports the Design Process
Elements.BodyText: AI tools assist designers by suggesting UI layouts, identifying design inconsistencies, and automating visual testing, enabling faster and more informed design decisions.
Elements.Notes: AI can analyze user behavior patterns to recommend interface improvements. In the context of this course, AI tools may help students generate initial design ideas or evaluate usability heuristics.

Items.Text: AI can suggest UI layouts and color schemes based on established user behavior data.
Automated visual testing tools use AI to detect design inconsistencies across devices.
AI recommendations should be treated as starting points, not final design decisions.

Elements.Title: AI Coding Assistants
Elements.BodyText: AI coding assistants like GitHub Copilot provide real-time code suggestions, generate boilerplate, explain code, and assist with debugging, helping developers work faster and with fewer errors.
Elements.Notes: GitHub Copilot is integrated directly into popular editors and can generate code from natural language prompts. Students should review all AI-generated code carefully before committing it.

Items.Text: AI coding tools suggest completions as developers type, reducing keyboarding effort.
Natural language prompts can generate functional code, tests, and documentation automatically.
AI-assisted code reviews can flag style inconsistencies and potential bugs before merging.
Developers must review AI-generated code critically—it can introduce bugs or security issues.

Elements.Title: AI Across the Software Development Lifecycle
Elements.BodyText: AI tools support every phase of the SDLC, from analyzing requirements and predicting risks in planning, to monitoring performance and fixing bugs after deployment.
Elements.Notes: Key SDLC phases where AI adds value: planning (requirement gap analysis, risk prediction), design (architecture recommendations), development (code generation, documentation), testing (automated test generation, vulnerability scanning), deployment (CI/CD management), and maintenance (anomaly detection).

Items.Text: In planning, AI can identify requirement gaps and predict project timeline risks.
During testing, AI automatically generates test cases and scans for security vulnerabilities.
Post-deployment, AI monitors system performance and predicts failures before users are affected.

Elements.Title: Responsible Use of AI in This Course
Elements.BodyText: While AI tools are encouraged as productivity aids, students are responsible for understanding, reviewing, and standing behind all AI-assisted work they submit.
Elements.Notes: Establish clear course norms: AI is a collaborator, not a substitute for understanding. Students should be able to explain any code or design decision, even if AI helped generate it. Document AI tool usage in commit messages or design notes where appropriate.

Items.Text: All AI-generated code must be read, understood, and verified by the student before use.
Over-reliance on AI without understanding can mask skill gaps that appear in assessments.
Intellectual property and licensing considerations apply to AI-generated content.
Documenting where and how AI tools were used promotes transparency and academic integrity.

Topics.Title: Development Environment Setup
Topics.Summary: Guides students through configuring their local and cloud-based development environments so that every team member can write, run, and collaborate on code from day one.

Elements.Title: Choosing a Code Editor
Elements.BodyText: A code editor is the primary tool through which developers write and manage code; selecting and configuring it correctly at the start of a project ensures consistency across the team.
Elements.Notes: VS Code is recommended for this course due to its extensive extension ecosystem, built-in Git support, and GitHub Copilot integration. Teams should agree on a shared set of extensions and settings.

Items.Text: VS Code is free, cross-platform, and widely used in both industry and education.
Extensions add language support, linters, formatters, and AI assistance to the editor.
Sharing a recommended extensions list in the repository ensures team consistency.

Elements.Title: Installing and Configuring Git Locally
Elements.BodyText: Git must be installed on each student's machine and configured with their identity before they can interact with the team's GitHub repository from the command line.
Elements.Notes: Students should run git config --global user.name and git config --global user.email to link their commits to their GitHub account. SSH key setup is recommended for secure, password-free authentication.

Items.Text: Git installation provides the command-line tools needed to clone, commit, and push code.
Configuring a username and email ties each commit to the correct contributor identity.
SSH key authentication is more secure than password-based HTTPS authentication.
The git clone command copies the remote repository to the local machine to begin work.

Elements.Title: Cloud Development with GitHub Codespaces
Elements.BodyText: GitHub Codespaces provides a full, cloud-based development environment accessible from any browser, eliminating setup inconsistencies across different machines and operating systems.
Elements.Notes: Codespaces launches in seconds and includes a configured VS Code instance with all dependencies. This is especially useful for teams where members have varying hardware or operating systems.

Items.Text: Codespaces runs in the cloud, so the local machine's operating system does not affect the environment.
A devcontainer configuration file can standardize the environment for all team members.
Codespaces integrates directly with the GitHub repository, making clone and commit seamless.

Elements.Title: Project Folder Structure and Conventions
Elements.BodyText: Establishing a consistent folder structure and naming convention at the start of the project reduces confusion, prevents merge conflicts, and makes the codebase easier to navigate for all team members.
Elements.Notes: Recommend a simple structure: /src for source code, /design for exported design assets, /docs for documentation, and /tests for test files. Agree on naming conventions such as kebab-case for files.

Items.Text: A documented folder structure should be described in the repository's README from day one.
Consistent file naming conventions prevent case-sensitivity errors across operating systems.
Separating source code, assets, documentation, and tests keeps the repository organized.

Elements.Title: Verifying the Complete Setup
Elements.BodyText: Before closing out the first module, every team member should verify that their full environment is working by completing a short end-to-end test: edit a file, commit it, push to GitHub, and confirm it appears in the shared repository.
Elements.Notes: This smoke test catches setup problems early—authentication errors, wrong email configurations, or permission issues—before they block work in week two. The instructor should build this into an in-class or lab activity.

Items.Text: An end-to-end test confirms that local Git, the editor, and GitHub are all communicating correctly.
Catching authentication or permission errors in week one prevents delays in later weeks.
Every team member must independently verify their own setup, not just one representative.

Topics.Title: Team Collaboration and Project Kickoff
Topics.Summary: Establishes team norms, assigns roles, and produces the initial project artifacts that will guide collaborative work throughout the course. Students leave this module with a shared project vision and operational infrastructure.

Elements.Title: Forming Effective Project Teams
Elements.BodyText: Project teams in this course are structured to mirror cross-functional product teams in industry, combining students with different strengths across design, development, and project coordination.
Elements.Notes: Discuss the value of diverse skill sets on a team. Even if all students are in the same program, individual strengths vary. Teams should surface these differences early and assign responsibilities accordingly.

Items.Text: Cross-functional teams produce better outcomes by combining diverse perspectives and skills.
Teams should identify each member's strengths in design, coding, communication, and research.
Establishing shared expectations early reduces friction and miscommunication later.

Elements.Title: Defining Team Roles and Responsibilities
Elements.BodyText: Assigning clear roles at the start of the project ensures accountability and prevents work from falling through the gaps during collaborative development.
Elements.Notes: Suggested roles: Project Lead (coordinates tasks and deadlines), Design Lead (owns Figma workspace), Dev Lead (owns GitHub repository and branching strategy), and Documentation Lead (maintains README and meeting notes). Roles may rotate in later modules.

Items.Text: Named roles create clear ownership and make it easier to resolve blockers quickly.
Roles should be documented in the repository so the entire team and instructor can reference them.
Responsibilities may be shared or rotated to ensure all students gain experience across areas.

Elements.Title: Creating the Team Charter
Elements.BodyText: A team charter is a brief agreement that documents the team's goals, working norms, communication channels, and conflict resolution approach before work begins.
Elements.Notes: The charter does not need to be formal. A shared document or a pinned GitHub Discussion works well. Key items: meeting cadence, preferred communication tool (e.g., Slack, Discord), decision-making process, and how to handle missed deadlines.

Items.Text: A team charter surfaces assumptions about working styles before they cause conflict.
Documenting communication channels ensures no team member is left out of key decisions.
Agreed-upon norms for deadlines and accountability reduce interpersonal friction.

Elements.Title: Scoping the Course Project
Elements.BodyText: Each team selects and defines the scope of their course project in week one, producing a brief problem statement and initial set of user goals that will drive the entire design and development process.
Elements.Notes: The project scope should be ambitious enough to apply HCI concepts meaningfully but narrow enough to complete in the course timeframe. A good scope statement identifies who the users are, what problem they face, and what a successful solution looks like.

Items.Text: A clear problem statement anchors all subsequent design and development decisions.
User goals describe what real people need to accomplish, not what the system will do.
Scope should be reviewed with the instructor before the team invests heavily in design work.

Elements.Title: End-of-Module Readiness Checklist
Elements.BodyText: By the end of this module, every team must have all project infrastructure operational and documented so that week two collaborative work can begin without setup delays.
Elements.Notes: Use this as a formative checkpoint. Teams that are missing items should resolve them before the next session. The checklist also gives students a concrete sense of accomplishment after a setup-heavy first module.

Items.Text: Each team member has a verified GitHub account with access to the shared repository.
The Figma Education team workspace is created and all members are invited.
Local development environments are installed, configured, and smoke-tested by every member.
The team charter and project scope statement are documented and stored in the repository.
